talks.title: io_uring: So Fast. It's Scary.
talks.teaser: Details io_uring: So Fast. Its Scary and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Overview: A presenter at Linux Security Summit Europe delivers a deep dive on io_uring, Linux's high-performance asynchronous I/O interface, examining its security implications.

Key Topics: io_uring as asynchronous I/O replacing synchronous syscall overhead; submission and completion queues; shared memory rings between kernel and userspace; and security considerations for the attack surface.

Technical Details: The talk explains io_uring's architecture where applications submit multiple I/O requests without waiting, using shared ring buffers for kernel-userspace communication. The speaker notes this replaces traditional open/read/write syscall paths.

Takeaways: io_uring's performance benefits come with a new attack surface via shared kernel-userspace memory. Security researchers and defenders should audit io_uring usage in privileged applications.

talks.title: Flexible Array Transformations and Array-bounds Checking - Gustavo A. R. Silva, The Linux Foundation
talks.teaser: Evaluates flexible Array Transformations and Array-bounds Checking - Gustavo A. R. Silva, The Linux Foundation and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Kernel Background

Gustavo Silva of the Linux kernel self-protection project and Google OSS security explains how C arrays, trailing arrays, and flexible structures underpin much kernel code—and many bugs.

Flexible Array History

Kernel code historically declared variable-length trailing data using one-element or zero-length array hacks predating C99 flexible array members. One-element arrays skew size calculations and invite off-by-one allocation mistakes.

True vs Fake Flex Arrays

C99 flexible array members are the standards-based approach, unlike GNU zero-length extensions or deprecated one-element patterns. Silva shows why developers must subtract phantom element sizes or use struct_size helpers when allocating.

Project Goals

Multiple incompatible flexible-array styles block reliable bounds checking across the tree. The ongoing transformation work audits size usage, updates user API call sites, and aims to remove ambiguity so the kernel can enforce safer array access.

talks.title: HotBPF - An On-demand and On-the-fly Memory Protection for the Linux Ker... Yueqi Chen & Zhenpeng Li
talks.teaser: Analyzes hotBPF - An On-demand and On-the-fly Memory Protection for the Linux Ker... Yueqi Chen & Zhenpeng Li and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
Motivation and threat window

Yueqi Chen and Zhenpeng Li present HotBPF, on-demand kernel memory protection for slab-allocated objects without recompiling or rebooting. They highlight the roughly 66-day average gap between vulnerability discovery and patch deployment when attackers can freely develop exploits.

Slab exploitation model

Use-after-free and out-of-bounds writes on slab objects let attackers corrupt adjacent victims and hijack function pointers. HotBPF isolates vulnerable objects in the non-overlapping vmalloc region so associated corruption cannot reach victims in direct-map slab memory.

Design and implementation

Challenges include pinpointing specific vulnerable structs among thousands of types without over-separating. A userspace agent parses fuzzer or static-analysis bug reports and stack traces, maps allocation sites via debug info, and loads eBPF hooks to divert vulnerable-object allocations dynamically at runtime.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Yueqi (Louis) Chen, Assistant Professor at the University of Colorado Boulder, presents "HotBPF" alongside co-author Zhenpeng Li (Northwestern University), developed in collaboration with researchers at IBM Watson Research Center and Virginia Tech. The presentation addresses the critical 66-day vulnerability window between bug discovery and patch deployment in the Linux kernel. To mitigate heap memory corruptions without requiring kernel recompilation or system reboots, the authors present HotBPF, an on-demand, live memory protection system powered by extended Berkeley Packet Filters (eBPF) and dynamic binary instrumentation.

Key Topics:
- The 66-day vulnerability-to-patch exposure window in upstream and downstream Linux kernels
- Mechanics of slab-based heap exploitation (Use-After-Free, heap spraying, and cross-cache attacks)
- Automated root-cause and allocation site identification using crash call traces and backward taint analysis
- Live-patching and memory isolation via eBPF trampolines, int3 software breakpoints, and dedicated memory pools

Technical Details:
Chen explains that the lifecycle of kernel vulnerabilities introduces a protracted exposure window averaging 66 days between bug reporting (via KASAN, syzbot, or static analysis) and patch deployment. During this interval, attackers exploit slab-allocator vulnerabilities—primarily Use-After-Free (UAF) and out-of-bounds corruptions—by executing heap sprays to groom freed memory slots and overwrite sensitive function pointers. Traditional live patching (such as kpatch) requires manual, error-prone C patch development, while recompiling and rebooting production servers incurs unacceptable downtime. HotBPF resolves this by automating temporary heap isolation directly from existing bug reports.

The system's pipeline operates in two stages. First, an automated analysis tool inspects crash reports and call traces generated by native debugging panics or KASAN checks. By performing backward taint analysis on critical conditional check variables, HotBPF traces memory access back to the root vulnerable structure (for example, identifying `tun_file` as the vulnerable object enclosing an `napi_struct`). It then maps source-level allocation sites to runtime binary addresses using DWARF debugging symbols. Second, HotBPF synthesizes an eBPF protection program and deploys it live into the running kernel. It instruments kernel allocation (`kmalloc`, `kmem_cache_alloc`) and free functions by rewriting call instructions with `int3` software interrupts or BPF trampolines. HotBPF intercepts allocations of the identified vulnerable objects and redirects them into dedicated, isolated memory regions (such as distinct `vmalloc` spaces or isolated slab caches), preventing attackers from overlapping freed slots with sprayed objects. On deallocation, HotBPF queries an eBPF map (~1,500 ns) and updates object state (~6,000 ns), neutralizing double-free attempts.

Key Takeaways:
HotBPF proves that eBPF combined with dynamic binary patching can successfully shield the Linux kernel from heap exploitation without downtime or recompilation. Evaluated against 46 real-world kernel bug reports, HotBPF achieved zero false negatives (FN = 0) with negligible operational overhead under standard LMbench benchmarks compared to standard system call latencies (e.g., 420,000 ns for `read`). Enterprise infrastructure teams can leverage automated eBPF heap isolation to defend production systems during the sensitive vulnerability disclosure window, though specialized hardware allocations like DMA buffers remain design limitations requiring physical memory contiguity.

talks.title: Device Attestation in Hardware TEE based Confidential Computing
talks.teaser: Examines device Attestation in Hardware TEE based Confidential Computing and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary:
## Confidential Computing Context

Arjun Nakajima and Joel present device attestation for hardware TEE-based confidential computing, a prerequisite for TEE I/O (assigning devices to trusted VMs like Intel TDX). Direct device assignment is not yet available for hardware TEE VMs, making attestation the critical first step.

## TDISP Architecture

The talk introduces the Trusted Device Interface Security Protocol (TDISP). Key entities include the TSM (TEE Security Manager) in the platform trust boundary and the DSM (Device Security Manager) on each device, communicating over a secure channel.

## Two Attestation Challenges

First, the TEE must verify device identity via X.509 certificate chains and firmware measurements (SVM) against policy manifests. Second, it must validate dynamic interface configuration—capabilities, MMIO mappings, and other VMM-assigned settings attackers could spoof.

## Data Protection Models

For TEE I/O use cases, standard PCR-based identity streams protect DMA paths; for TEE device models, bounce-buffer encryption uses negotiated keys. The speakers position attestation as foundational plumbing before confidential VMs can safely use physical devices.
